Loquacious means talking a lot, often more than what the situation really calls for. When you describe someone as loquacious, you are saying they have a strong tendency to speak at length, go into great detail, and keep the conversation going — even when others might prefer a shorter answer or a moment of silence.

Think of that one person you know who, when you ask "How was your weekend?", gives you a full 20-minute story with every tiny detail included. That person is loquacious.

This is important, because knowing a word's feeling is just as important as knowing its definition.

Loquacious is slightly negative, but gently so. It is not a harsh insult — it is more like a mild, polite criticism, or even a teasing observation. When someone calls a person loquacious, they are usually rolling their eyes a little, but with a smile. It sounds almost too formal and fancy to be a truly mean word.

It is worth noting that loquacious is not a neutral word the way "tall" or "blue" is. It always carries that subtle suggestion that the person talks a bit too much. However, it can also be used affectionately — for example, a grandparent who tells long, winding stories might lovingly be called loquacious by their grandchildren.

Here are some sentences that show exactly how loquacious works in practice:

  • "My loquacious uncle dominated the entire dinner conversation — nobody else could get a word in."
  • "She became surprisingly loquacious after the nervousness wore off."
  • "The professor was so loquacious that he never finished the lesson plan — he kept going off on long tangents."
  • "Even in his emails, he was loquacious — a simple yes-or-no question would get a five-paragraph reply."

Notice in these examples that loquacious always points to the same core idea: the person talks or expresses themselves far beyond what is necessary.
How It Compares to Similar Words

Understanding how loquacious sits among similar words will make its meaning crystal clear.

Talkative is the most neutral option. It simply means a person talks a lot. No judgment attached. You could call a cheerful, friendly child "talkative" and it sounds completely positive.

Chatty is warm and informal. It suggests friendly, casual conversation. Calling someone chatty is almost always a compliment, or at worst completely harmless.

Loquacious sits a step beyond talkative. It implies the talking is a little excessive, a little hard to stop, and can sometimes be tiring for the listener. It is more formal and literary than chatty or talkative.

Garrulous is the more extreme and more negative version. A garrulous person talks endlessly, often about trivial or pointless things, and people around them are clearly worn out by it. Garrulous is a stronger criticism than loquacious.

So if you picture a scale of "talks a lot," it might look like this:

Chatty → Talkative → Loquacious → Garrulous

Loquacious lives comfortably in the middle-to-upper range — noticeable and slightly excessive, but not insufferable.

It is easy to mix this word up, so here is what it does not mean:

  • It does not mean intelligent or eloquent. A loquacious person is not necessarily saying anything wise or well-crafted — they are simply saying a lot.
  • It does not mean loud. A loquacious person can speak in a soft, quiet voice. The quantity of words is what matters, not the volume.
  • It does not mean rude or obnoxious. There is no aggression in the word. It is about length and frequency of speech, not the manner of it.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

If you need one sentence to lock this word in your memory:

A loquacious person never uses one word when ten will do.

That captures it perfectly. They fill silence with words, extend conversations well past their natural endpoint, and always have more to say. It is a word that almost sounds like what it means — something about the way it rolls along, lo-QUAY-shus, feels like it just keeps going.
